query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Short-range local chemical ordering in five-element Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles broadens their premelting regime by stabilizing partial surface melts at lower temperatures, causing a multi-step melting sequence that precedes the abrupt melting of their single-element counterparts.
generation.material_initial_state: As-synthesized single-phase Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles of uniform size (e.g., 5–20 nm), retained by rapid cooling from a previous high-temperature process.
generation.intervention: Controlled heating from room temperature to above the melting range with in-situ high-resolution TEM and parallel molecular-dynamics simulations to resolve atomic rearrangements and track phase transformations in real time.
generation.conditions: Identical heating ramp rates are applied to the high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles and to a baseline single-metal or binary nanoparticle system of comparable size under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Development of transient compositional heterogeneities—domains of slightly different local elemental ratios—at near-surface regions.
generation.mechanism: These transient heterogeneities reduce local free energy barriers, leading to early surface melting that gradually transitions inward. The chemical complexity and partial short-range order collectively stabilize the molten layer, extending the premelting interval and delaying complete molten collapse.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the single or binary baseline particles, the high-entropy Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles show a broader premelting region with a lower onset temperature for partial surface melting, yet an overall delayed final melting point due to the multi-element entropic stabilization.
generation.baseline: Monometallic (e.g., pure Ni) or binary (Fe–Ni) nanoparticles of similar size and morphology, subjected to the same thermal cycle, will display a sharper and more abrupt melting transition in the same experimental setup.
generation.boundary: This mechanism should manifest for 5–20 nm HEA nanoparticles with minimal surface oxidation and under moderate heating rates (e.g., < 100 K/min). Strong surface oxidation or extremely rapid heating/cooling may alter the premelting pathway.
generation.uncertainty: While partial local ordering is hypothesized to play a key role, quantitative characterization of atomic-scale segregation at high temperatures remains challenging, and exact onset temperatures for partial and complete melting cannot be precisely predicted at present.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform repeated heating experiments under in-situ transmission electron microscopy, comparing Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles with single-metal or binary nanoparticles of the same size distribution and shape. Use identical heating profiles and observe the onset and progression of partial and full melting in real time.
measurements: Real-time lattice-resolved TEM imaging to detect partial surface melting (appearance of liquid-like shells or loss of crystallinity) and subsequent full melting
High-speed electron diffraction or in-situ X-ray diffraction to measure the broadening of phase transitions
Quantification of local chemical composition via EDS or EELS at different stages of heating
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles show (a) no earlier onset of surface melting than single-metal controls, or (b) no broadening in the premelting regime, contrary to the proposed short-range ordering mechanism, the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This simple model of particle formation demonstrates that adding more elements innately promotes a more random nanoparticle, regardless of element interactions. Naturally, this model offers an idealized perspective and does not reflect all experimental details. In reality, there will be distinct mixing enthalpies between the elements. This will introduce a preference for certain structures which is opposed by the limited mobility of atoms. This explains how a rather mixed particle is obtained in the synthesis for a five-element mixture, which is restricted in the binary case, but also sees signs of local segregation in the NMF analysis. The model relates well to the single-source precursor synthesis, where a solid precursor is reduced at moderate temperatures, hence limiting the free mobility. Extending this approach to other syntheses with similar solid, mixed precursors can thus provide a viable way to design new low-temperature approaches for small high entropy alloy nanoparticles. It can further be argued that starting with a high number of different elements favors the exploration of high-entropy material spaces. Simultaneous in situ X-ray diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy experiments allowed us to study the formation mechanism of noble metal bimetallic and high entropy alloy nanoparticles in depth. The samples were prepared by reduction of single-source precursors. For five-element mixtures, the formation of a single phase occurs more readily than in the binary samples. Under the studied reaction conditions, single-phase formation for binary alloys was restricted to systems where cooperative reduction occurred, while single-phase HEA particles could be obtained even though the elements were reduced consecutively. The findings are explained with a stochastic model that simulates the particle formation process. Regardless of the element interactions, the model quantifies that it is more likely to form a random alloy if more atom types are present in a system with limited free atom mobility. This highlights that knowledge of the formation mechanism is crucial for understanding the material formation pathways.
